How NPR+ fits into the public media business model : Planet Money NPR launched NPR+ to give podcast listeners (a.k.a. you) a way to support public media. But how does the NPR+ business model actually work?
On today’s show, we look under the hood of our subscriptions business: unpacking where the money goes, what it means to us at Planet Money, and how our little corner of the podcast economy works. We’ll also explain why NPR is winding down Planet Money+ and other single-show subscriptions.
This was originally released as a Planet Money bonus episode. We’re sharing it now with everyone in the feed.
You can learn more about NPR+ here.

Macy's flagship store in New York unveils its 2026 holiday display.
Eugene Gologursky/Getty Images
hide caption
Eugene Gologursky/Getty Images
Sign up for alerts on breaking news and exclusive reporting from NPR
Leaving the Macy's flagship store in New York, the Niesig family visiting from Germany sizes up their loot: a pair of sweatpants for mom, a Hurley jacket for dad, Ugg boots for their daughter. Son Mika, 16, is the only one empty-handed.
"I like zipper hoodies, and there was one zipper from Levi's that was pretty cool," he says. "But in the end, I didn't buy it because it was just a little boring."
Only on NPR
What to know before using AI agents for Black Friday shopping
As Macy's this week celebrates the 100th edition of its Thanksgiving Day Parade, the department store finds itself at a turning point. After years of questionable financial prospects, Macy's is trying to reinvent — as a luxury destination.
The retailer's gambit is to keep its old shoppers while also attracting new customers, who will perhaps pay more for real leather and upscale brands.
How Macy's got squeezed in the middle
Long before the pandemic, Macy's was grappling with America's shrinking middle class — and its own lack of fresh vision.
The department store business, to begin with, has become challenging. Big store space is expensive. Online competition is stiff. Shoppers are increasingly buying directly from their favorite brands.
And Macy's faces its own struggle. The chain is neither a discounter like Kohl's or T.J.Maxx, nor an upscale store like Bergdorf Goodman or Nordstrom. Macy's has languished in between.
Pop Culture
Here's how the Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade is brought to life
"They were kind of like right in the middle," says Michael Prendergast, who advises retailers and brands at the consulting firm Alvarez & Marsal. "Now over time, that middle tier basically got crushed."
When the pandemic hit, store closures had Macy's forecasting an estimated $1.1 billion in losses. Its stock value dropped so low that the company was kicked off the big-league index, the S&P 500.
The way out is up
At one point, Macy's seemed to throw every other thing on discount just to get people buying something.
But it didn't work.
A shopper with a bag from rival Target visits Macy's in New York.
Michael M. Santiago/Getty Images
hide caption
Michael M. Santiago/Getty Images
Stores looked disheveled and chaotic. Shoppers regularly noted a lack of workers to help on the floor. Over 2023, sales at Macy's dropped almost 7%.
Soaring inflation all but forced Macy's hand.
As the so-called K-shaped economy split the nation in recent years, folks with less money turned to Walmart or Target, which stepped up their game. Wealthier people continued to be the ones doing most of the spending, but also not at Macy's — leaning toward higher-end shops.
"For their size and scale the choice is almost made for them," says Prendergast, who's spent 20 years in the fashion business, including selling to Macy's at Tommy Hilfiger.
"If you're Macy's you say, 'We're still getting squeezed in the middle, our customer base in the U.S. is getting squeezed in the middle. Where can we go?' And really the only answer is to go up."
The new luxury vision
Luxury is now the big Macy's bet.
The retailer already owns the upscale Bloomingdale's, with its designer brands. Macy's also owns the luxury beauty chain Bluemercury.
In 2024, the head of Bloomingdale's took over the entire Macy's company and announced a turnaround plan, " A Bold New Chapter."
Planet Money Newsletter
Has the economy gone C-shaped?
It included closing 150 stores and upgrading more than 300 others. Changes were proposed for the website and the staffing. Stores began to tackle clutter and add nicer items.
"We needed to remove the duplication, the redundancy," says Julie Walsh, senior vice president at Macy's whose team buys women's accessories and beauty products, including shoes, jewelry and makeup.
"When you come onto our floor now, it's a little bit lighter," she says. "So that the product that is on the floor shows up in a meaningful way."
Putting the higher prices to the test
In March, Macy's finally reported a year of growing sales.
The higher-end Bloomingdale's stores continued to drive much of the company's growth, but changes seemed to start paying off at Macy's, too.
Fancier options — like real leather instead of faux, brands like Ralph Lauren and Coach — have been raising the retailer's average selling price. It increased 9% in the latest quarter, executives said in September. They described shoppers' visits as "very steady and very significant."
A mall visitor walks into a Macy's department store in Towson, Md.
Stephanie Scarbrough/AP
hide caption
Stephanie Scarbrough/AP
Barb Anderson-Kerlin, a loyal Macy's shopper checking out the retailer's flagship in New York, says she's noticed a difference at the chain, after years of finding stores that seemed to ramble in all directions.

How far can luxury sales take Macy's?
Still, most shoppers at the flagship store appeared dubious of the image of Macy's as a high-end chain.

U.S. Judge: FCC violated ABC’s free speech to please Trump : NPR
Accessibility links

Keyboard shortcuts for audio player
U.S. Judge: FCC violated ABC’s free speech to please Trump A federal judge has blocked the Trump administration from moving to review all local broadcast licenses held by ABC. The stations air in six of the largest U.S. markets.
Media
U.S. Judge rules FCC violated ABC's free speech rights to please Trump
November 26, 202612:23 AM ET
Heard on Morning Edition
David Folkenflik
U.S. judge rules FCC violated ABC’s free speech rights to please Trump
Listen
1:35
1:35
Transcript
Download
Embed
<iframe src="https://www.npr.org/player/embed/nx-s1-6000576/nx-s1-10020775" width="100%" height="290" frameborder="0" scrolling="no" title="NPR embedded audio player">
Transcript
Under Chairman Brendan Carr, left, the Federal Communications Commission launched an early review of Disney's licenses to operate all the local ABC stations it owns. New Disney CEO Josh D'Amaro, right, says the company is fighting back to protect ABC's journalistic integrity and free speech. "We're very principled on this," he said.
Heather Diehl/Thibault Camus/Pool/AFP via Getty Images
hide caption
Heather Diehl/Thibault Camus/Pool/AFP via Getty Images
A federal judge has blocked President Trump and his administration from taking action to challenge the ABC television network's broadcast licenses, finding it to be an unconstitutional punishment for satire, commentary and news coverage that Trump doesn't like.
Media
Disney, ABC battle Trump's FCC in court over free speech protections
In her preliminary injunction filed Wednesday, U.S. District Court Judge Loren AliKhan found that the federal agency's early reviews represented retaliation for speech the Trump administration resented.
Such perceived offenses included late-night host Jimmy Kimmel's jabs at the president, the critical remarks of hosts on the chat show The View, and the moderation of a presidential debate in September 2024.
ABC and its corporate parent, the Walt Disney Co., serve six of the 10 largest markets in the U.S., including New York, Los Angeles, and Houston. They contribute significantly to the network's bottom line.
"Given the extreme, indeed existential, nature of the possible penalty Plaintiffs face -- loss of their broadcast licenses -- the court concludes that early license renewal proceedings create a risk sufficient to chill a broadcaster of ordinary firmness," Judge AliKhan wrote.
She rejected the Trump administration's motion to dismiss the lawsuit from ABC and Disney challenging the review of the local licenses. Usually the licenses last eight years and are up for review on a staggered basis. They are rarely taken away.
In her ruling, AliKhan relied heavily on public statements and social media postings in which Trump attacked ABC and Disney, as well as posts by Trump's pick as the chair of the Federal Communications Commission, Brendan Carr.
"What started in 2020 as questions about how ABC 'can keep getting a license' if it 'report[s] fake news,' ... has crescendoed into repeated calls for the Commission to strip ABC's broadcast licenses for their editorial decisions," she wrote. "The court counts eleven such calls made by President Trump over the past two years -- the most recent being in July 2026."
And the judge cited the administration's "tangible steps toward enforcing President Trump and Commissioner Carr's repeated threats to strip the Plaintiff Stations of their licenses."
"Chairman Carr has taken President Trump's rhetoric as his marching orders," Judge AliKhan wrote.
Carr did not respond to NPR's request for comment Wednesday evening.
ABC hailed the ruling in a statement as "an important victory for the First Amendment."
Among the targets of ire from Trump and Carr was ABC's decision not to broadcast Trump's July 2026 Oval Office address on its television network. ABC's legal team said the network streamed it on its digital news service, but would not have done so absent the political pressure from the FCC.
It is one of several examples of newsroom decisions made under duress, the network's lawyers said in court. Kimmel's interview with then-Democratic U.S. Senate nominee James Talarico of Texas was uploaded to YouTube instead of being aired on ABC's late night television show. (Talarico won election to the U.S. Senate earlier this month.) And The View stopped hosting candidates for political office in 2026 in the months ahead of the fall elections.
Media
FCC Democrat says Disney 'has found its courage' in lawsuit against agency
Judge AliKhan rejected arguments from the FCC that the court could not take action because it has not yet rejected the license renewals. The very act of premature review for retaliatory reasons is unconstitutional and unlawful – and hard to reverse, she wrote.
"For nearly two years, the agency has weaponized its licensing authority to retaliate against broadcasters for exercising their right to free expression, and now a federal court has stepped in to put a check on that conduct," said Anna M. Gomez, the lone Democratic commissioner on the FCC. "Every broadcaster facing this pressure should take note and choose courage over capitulation because, as I've said from the beginning, the First Amendment is on their side."
This ruling comes six weeks after a parallel ruling in a case brought by CNN, MS NOW and Politico against the Trump administration for restricting access. Officials barred journalists from the three news outlets from the White House after Trump lambasted them for " purposefully negative" news coverage.
In that case, U.S. District Court Judge Timothy Kelly issued a preliminary injunction, writing, "It is not hard to conclude that President Trump likely banned Plaintiffs from the White House because he believes that their reporting is generally inaccurate and biased against him." That, he wrote, represents a form of unlawful retaliation. The administration is appea

What to know before using AI agents for Black Friday shopping 59% of U.S. shoppers plan to use AI for holiday shopping this weekend, according to the National Retail Federation
What to know before using AI agents for Black Friday shopping
November 25, 20268:51 AM ET
Heard on Morning Edition
By
Stephan Bisaha
What to know before using AI agents for Black Friday shopping
Listen
4:50
4:50
Transcript
Download
Embed
<iframe src="https://www.npr.org/player/embed/nx-s1-6048524/nx-s1-10020783" width="100%" height="290" frameborder="0" scrolling="no" title="NPR embedded audio player">
Transcript
A pop-up shop for "dots" a personal assistant agent at the OpenAI developers conference on September 29, 2026 in San Francisco, California. Sam Altman announced a new artificial intelligence personal assistant agents named "dots" to rival Meta's Muse.
Heather Diehl/Getty Images
hide caption
Heather Diehl/Getty Images
Artificial intelligence is here to help with Black Friday.
This weekend, 59% of consumers plan on using AI to support their winter shopping, according to the National Retail Federation.
But AI has proven one way it is not unlike humans: It makes mistakes. The stakes of those hallucinations are much higher when your wallet – and holiday unwrapping memories – are on the line. These tools also become better shoppers when you hand over personal data, which also means giving up more information on your private life to massive tech companies.
Here are some tips – and notes of caution – before using AI as your personal holiday shopper.
Treat AI searches like a conversation with a kid
Traditional online shopping is about search terms and the infinite product scroll. AI is meant to be a conversation.
Unlike shopping on a retail website, AI platforms are designed to look more like texting apps. Prompt bars on these platforms sit on the bottom of the page, inviting a back and forth chat between user and bot about what to buy.
After all, it can be hard to know what keyword to plug in to shop for uncle before the Christmas exchange. AI instead allows for search based on a vibe – like describing that uncle's hobbies and personal style. If a shopper wants to buy a suitcase to support their uncle's European travel dreams, this makes it easier to narrow down the options.
"You can say if that bag is overstuffed, will it fit under the seat on JetBlue?" says Emily Pfeiffer, a principal analyst at Forrester who advises retailers and brands on digital commerce strategy, including for AI. "Don't give me the dimensions," she advises, "Tell me if it will suit my use case."
Pfeiffer cautions that even though AI is able to think through these nuanced shopping criteria, it works better with more hand holding.
"It's best if you imagine that it's a young child who will probably misinterpret your request," Pfeiffer said. "You want to be as specific and clear as possible."
AI Agents can shop for you. Be careful what you give them
Newer AI models can do more than talk and brainstorm. They can handle shopping tasks.
If shoppers are, for example, worried about holiday shipments arriving on time, AI can monitor an email inbox in order to track packages, even messaging a late shipper on the shopper's behalf. Beyond just suggesting a gift, agents can do the actual buying (with your money).
These are useful features, but require granting access to sensitive personal data, such as an inbox or credit card. One of the first questions Meta's AI agent platform Muse asks is if the user would like to connect their email and calendar.
Meta says its AI is highly secure. Everyone is assigned their own AI agent and the company promises that information shoppers share with it is kept private. Particularly sensitive information like credit card numbers, they say, are held separately and never viewed directly by the AI.
Yet Meta also has long been accused of violating user privacy, as in a 2022 case about improperly sharing user data. Meta did not admit to wrongdoing but settled for about $725 million.
Technology
Facebook parent Meta will pay $725M to settle a privacy suit over Cambridge Analytica
Beyond Meta, there are cases of AI jumping guardrails that programmers set for it. Users have also reported their AI agents acting without their consent, such as sending their home address to a buyer from Facebook Marketplace and booking a hotel.
Technology
Meta's Muse: Killer app? Security nightmare? Both?
Philip Bruno, chief strategy and growth officer with ACI Worldwide, says he would share what he's shopping for with AI, but warns to be more careful with personal information.
"I'm cooking for a family of four. That is fine to be able to say," Bruno says. "I would be very careful about payment information."
On that note, experts caution shoppers to be careful with other people's information. It's easy to give most AIs loads of information about your father while brainstorming his gift. Know AI agents can also use this to build profiles of the shopper's friends and family. Being elusive and not specifying who you're shopping for during the brainstorming can help.
Just like for humans, it takes time for AI to find the best deals
One major selling point for using AI agents is that they can check multiple websites and compare prices, bringing them for human review all in one spot. That does not mean the first price it shows you is the best one.
"One of the biggest misconceptions about AI is that it somehow sees everything," Pfeiffer says. "That's just false. It gets you the best answer it can as quickly as possible."
Economy
Rising costs leave consumers looking for Thanksgiving bargains
AI agents still need time to hunt for deals. Many will often let shoppers watch along as they browse the web, rather than relying on preset knowledge.
This automating can also mean time savings for the user. Agents often can ru

articles.title: Buying new things feels wonderful. But it can also be a trap
articles.text:
How to break the cycle of constantly buying new things : NPR
Accessibility links
Skip to main content
Keyboard shortcuts for audio player
How to break the cycle of constantly buying new things Constantly buying new things can be problematic, says journalist Eric Athas, author of the new book "Saying No to New." Here's how to break the cycle and find joy in what you already have.
Buying new things feels wonderful. But it can also be a trap
November 25, 20265:02 AM ET
Andee Tagle
Eric Athas, author of the new book Saying No to New, says that "you do feel joy and excitement" from buying new things initially — "but science says those feelings can't last."
ㅤ/J Studios/Getty Images
hide caption
ㅤ/J Studios/Getty Images
Never miss a story or episode from Life Kit.  Sign up for our weekly newsletter to get our journalism delivered directly to your inbox.
Buyer beware: Holiday shopping season is here. Is every sale calling your name? Is your virtual shopping cart overflowing?
Before you start buying everything, take note. There's a reason new things get us excited, says Eric Athas, author of Saying No to New: Why New Things Are Stealing Your Time, Money, and Happiness — and How to Take Back Your Life, published in September. Our brains are wired to seek out newness, and the retail industry is set up to keep us coming back for more as quickly as possible.
Life Kit
Listen to the podcast version of this story
That constant consumption of novel possessions — whether they're brand-new, digital, secondhand or even free — can be problematic. "It's hard to be grateful for what you have if you're always on the lookout for something else," he says.
To break the cycle of chasing newness, we need to shop with more intention and find joy in what we already own, Athas says. In a conversation with Life Kit, he explains how. This interview has been edited for length and clarity.
Why are we so drawn to seeking out new things?
Our brains are programmed to find new things interesting and old things boring.
If you think about our ancient ancestors, it was beneficial [for their survival] to explore new foods to eat and new territory and eventually explore different parts of the world.
There's also research that shows when we encounter something new, we get a little shot of dopamine. You get that feeling of excitement when you first use that new app or try that new video game or bring home a new gizmo for the kitchen.
What are some of the downsides of chasing newness?
New things can steal our happiness. Everyone can relate to the feeling of tearing open that new box or putting on that new outfit. You do feel joy and excitement from that initially.
But science says those feelings can't last. So we have to go out and get something else, and that's where we can get into this cycle of constantly chasing happiness in new things.
These days, it feels particularly hard to focus on what you have. There's so much pressure to buy new things. Why is that?
Life Kit
How to hide your spending habits from retailers (so you don't get ripped off)
Everywhere we go, whether that's scrolling our favorite shopping app or browsing the aisle of our favorite store, there are little cues driving our [shopping] decisions.  These companies have designs we don't even realize are engineering our choices.
For example, at the  checkout page of a website or an app, there  might be a countdown clock that says, "Save 25% if you make this purchase in three minutes." That's a tactic meant to whip up anxiety.
The other part of this is that you can buy new things faster than you've ever been able to before. It's all seamless and frictionless.
Life Kit
Don't fall for these marketing tactics this holiday season
One way to shop more mindfully? Expand the "time and distance between you encountering a new thing and you acquiring it," Athas says. Do this by deleting a retailer's app, removing credit card information from a retail website or leaving an item in your cart for 24 hours before purchasing.
J Studios/Getty Images
hide caption
J Studios/Getty Images
What can we do to create more friction between ourselves and the new things we want to buy?
Expand what I call "the new-thing gap."  That's the time and distance between you encountering a new thing and you acquiring it.
If you've got one-click checkout with a certain company, maybe delete the app from your phone or remove your credit card information from that app.
Another easy tactic is to drop something in your cart and leave it there for 24 hours. Researchers have found that when you delay a purchase, interest in that thing will start to decline.
What happens when you use all these tactics and still feel like buying something new?
The main thing is to make intentional choices. The goal here is not to say no to all new things.
Life Kit
Why going on a 'say no' retreat is a gift to your future self
Now that I know my brain is programmed to find new things, I bring my attention to that whenever I feel drawn to something new. Is this something I want, or am I being influenced?
You can get really good at saying no to the wrong type of new things, better at saying yes to the right type of new things.
You say because we're programmed to want new things, we can be quick to set old things aside.  So is it possible to get joy from old things?
Research has found that if we force ourselves to revisit old things, we may find there's untapped enjoyment in those old things.
In one study, researchers had people go through a museum exhibit. At the end, they asked participants how much they thought they would enjoy going through the exhibit again. People predicted they would get less enjoyment from the repeated experience.
But when the researchers forced them to go through it again, the participants said, "Actually, we enjoyed that just as much, if not more, the second time." They discovered details they missed the first time around or just liked seeing everything again.
How do we apply this lesson in our own life?
Reexpe

articles.text:
Cannabis prices decline, due to discounts and oversupply : NPR
Accessibility links
Skip to main content
Keyboard shortcuts for audio player
Cannabis prices decline, due to discounts and oversupply Steep discounts for "Green Wednesday," one of the highest-selling days for cannabis, help customers keep costs down. But experts say retailers are feeling the pinch.
National
In a time of rising costs, one Thanksgiving commodity is cheaper: cannabis
November 25, 20265:00 AM ET
Heard on All Things Considered
By
Marissa J. Lang
In a time of rising costs, one Thanksgiving commodity is cheaper: cannabis
Listen
3:58
3:58
Transcript
Download
Embed
<iframe src="https://www.npr.org/player/embed/nx-s1-6046173/nx-s1-10020240" width="100%" height="290" frameborder="0" scrolling="no" title="NPR embedded audio player">
Transcript
Customers buy products at the Harvest Medical Marijuana Dispensary in San Francisco in 2016.
Haven Daley/AP
hide caption
Haven Daley/AP
This Thanksgiving season, Americans are paying more for almost everything: travel costs have soared, and the price of food has risen. Bringing wine to the family dinner? That costs more, too.
But there's one thing consumers buy at high rates that will actually get cheaper this time of year: marijuana.
Known in the industry as "Green Week" or "Green Wednesday," the days ahead of Thanksgiving have come to rival famed stoner holiday 4/20 as the day cannabis dispensaries see the most sales — and highest foot traffic — of the year.
In most dispensaries around the country, that means steep discounts, doorbuster specials and exclusive products. It's a good deal for customers, who line up in long queues as they await their turn with the so-called budtenders behind the counter.
Cannabis in the U.S. is a $30 billion industry with legal marketplaces in 24 states and the nation's capital, according to Whitney Economics, a firm that specializes in economic research and consulting on the business of cannabis. But in recent years, the deep discounts that have drawn in customers — and kept them coming back for weeks like this one — have squeezed retailers and resulted in a revenue decline in the legal market.
As the week began at The Forest, a dispensary in Baltimore, shoppers were stocking up for the holiday week.
A pack of gummies to bring to Friendsgiving in lieu of alcohol. A sparkling THC-infused beverage for those canna-curious in-laws. Or a holiday staple: some pre-rolls to share on an evening walk.
The Indicator from Planet Money
How Hemp-THC businesses are bracing for a near total ban
On bright screens posted around the store, discount offers flashed: 25% off edibles, read one; 30% off for medical patients, read another. An extra $5 off for bringing in cans of food for the store's holiday drive.
Kelley Vinton, 36, is a regular at The Forest. She's a medical marijuana user and usually sticks to a strict weekly budget, she said. But on Monday, she threw in a few little extras — for the "cousin walk," Vinton said.
"You know, you take a little breaky-poo with your cousins, and we live in the country, so we just walk, usually before dinner," Vinton said. "We smoke a joint, and we get nice and high, and get some munchies and get ready for dinner."
The federal government still classifies recreational marijuana as a Schedule I drug, meaning it is considered to have "high potential for abuse," according to the Drug Enforcement Administration. But medical cannabis was reclassified this year to Schedule III, a category shared by drugs like Tylenol with codeine and anabolic steroids.
In 2025, Whitney Economics found, revenue was down across the industry thanks to an oversupply of plant product and declining prices, driven by the discount culture of cannabis retailers.
National
Hemp and marijuana are the same species. So why all the different laws?
It was the first year since 2014 — when Colorado and Washington became the first states to legalize cannabis sales for recreational use — that the industry saw a dip, according to an analysis by Whitney Economics.
"It's forced a race to the bottom," said Beau Whitney, the founder and chief economist at Whitney Economics. "What this is resulting in is great prices for the consumer, they're spending less and getting the same or more, so that's good for them on an affordability perspective. But it's hurting operators."
Though the industry has seen a slight rebound this year — an increase of about 5% in sales for the same period last year, Whitney's team found — forecasts for the end of 2026 and the outlook for 2027 remain relatively modest.
The biggest reason for this, Whitney said, is customer behavior.
Through the beginning of the 2020s, Whitney said, consumers would typically come into a dispensary with a set amount to spend. Their cannabis budget. If they got a discount, Whitney said, they'd add additional products into their carts to hit their budget.
But that began to change in 2024, as inflation rose and the cost of essentials, like gas, ballooned.
"Behavior changed literally overnight," Whitney said. "What they're doing is they're taking the discounts — and there's a lot of them now — and they're using that money to buy gas and buy groceries. So they're adjusting the amount that they purchase based on what's going on in their own personal economy."
The discount model, he said, has also forced prices down. With legal retailers competing for a pool of customers that has not seen rapid growth in years, discounts help draw people into stores. But they've also created a culture where customers expect them, several cannabis store owners said.

Can weed help you drink less? Scientists study how well 'California sober' works
It's why doing well on a week like this one, as customers flood in for Green Wednesday deals, is essential for shop owners like The Forest's Christina Betancourt Johnson.
On Monday, the Baltimore store was stocked — with edibles and pre-rolls and other cannabis products, but also stacks of snacks
